opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important thing is to not let the competition define what we're doing. It's easy to look at the landscape and feel like every week there's a new model, a new benchmark, a new announcement, and the temptation is to just react. But the mission has always been to make sure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and that's a much longer game than any individual release cycle.

So the way I think about priorities is in a few layers. First, there's the research. We really believe that the core engine of progress is pushing the frontier of capability, and doing it in a way where safety and alignment are built in from the start, not bolted on afterward. You can't separate those two things. The systems that are most useful are the ones people can actually trust.

Second, there's deployment. One of the things we've learned is that you don't really understand a technology until it's out in the world and people are using it. Iterative deployment has been a cornerstone for us, because it lets society adapt alongside the technology, and it gives us real feedback on what's working and what isn't.

And third, there's compute and infrastructure. A lot of people underestimate how much of this is an engineering problem at enormous scale. Making sure we have the infrastructure to train and serve these models, and to do it reliably, is just as important as any algorithmic idea.

Honestly, I think competition is healthy. It pushes everyone to move faster and to think harder about doing things right. But for us, the question is always: are we making progress on the thing that actually matters, which is building something that is genuinely beneficial and broadly accessible? If we stay focused on that, I think the rest tends to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says competition should not define OpenAI’s work and centers its long-term mission and beneficial AI progress instead.

r002.rationale: It mentions making AI broadly accessible, but does not discuss ChatGPT’s free tier or explain why it was made widely available.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about constantly, and honestly I think the framing of "competitive landscape" can be a little misleading if you let it drive your decisions too much.

The way I think about it is: the mission hasn't changed. We're trying to build AGI that benefits all of humanity. And the thing that's shifted over the past few years is that a lot more people now believe that's possible, which means a lot more capital, a lot more talent, a lot more labs working on it. In some sense that's a good thing, right? It means the world is taking this seriously. But it also means we can't coast on being the only ones who care.

So when I look at priorities, I really break it into three buckets. The first is research. Can we keep pushing the frontier on what these systems can actually do? Reasoning, long-horizon tasks, agents that can go off and do real work for you reliably. That's where it all starts. If the research stalls, nothing else matters.

The second is turning that research into something people can actually use. One thing I've learned is that a capability sitting in a lab isn't worth much. The moment you put it in front of hundreds of millions of people, you learn things you never would have predicted, and you also create a kind of feedback loop that makes the next model better. Deployment is part of the research process, not something that happens after it.

And the third, which I think is the one that's easiest to deprioritize under competitive pressure, is safety and getting this right. Alignment, robustness, making sure we understand what these systems are doing. The temptation when everyone's racing is to say, we'll deal with that later. And I think the honest answer is that if you're not building those muscles now, you won't have them when the stakes are much higher.

On the competition itself, I'd say we try to be aware of it without being reactive to it. If you're just chasing whoever shipped something last week, you end up with a very incoherent strategy. We'd rather pick the few things we believe matter most, bet hard on them, and accept that sometimes someone else will have a flashier launch. What I don't want is for competitive dynamics to push the whole field toward cutting corners. That would be the worst outcome, not just for us, but for everyone.

And the last thing I'd say is, this is a very long game. Compute, infrastructure, the quality of the team, the trust you've built with users and with governments. Those compound over years. So the priority is really to keep making the kind of decisions that look good on a ten-year horizon, even when the quarterly scoreboard is noisy.

r001.rationale: The candidate centers the mission of building AGI that benefits humanity and says OpenAI should avoid reactive competition-driven decisions, prioritizing long-term choices instead.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses deploying research to many people, but does not mention ChatGPT’s free tier or explain its availability as a way to make AI accessible to everyone.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to stay focused on the mission: making sure AGI benefits all of humanity. Competition can push you to move faster, but it shouldn’t decide what you’re trying to accomplish.

For us, that means advancing the technology, doing the work to make it safe and reliable, and putting useful tools into people’s hands. Those priorities reinforce each other. When people use these systems, you learn what’s valuable, where they fall short, and what you need to improve.

So I’d focus less on winning any particular news cycle and more on whether we’re making meaningful progress. Are we helping people solve problems they couldn’t solve before? Are we understanding and addressing the risks as capabilities grow? That’s the standard we should hold ourselves to.

I think you have to start with the mission: making sure that AGI benefits all of humanity. Competition creates urgency, but it doesn’t tell you what you should be building or how you should deploy it.

For us, the priorities are advancing the technology, making it useful to people, and doing the safety work that lets us deploy responsibly. Those things reinforce each other. When people use the systems, we learn where they’re valuable, where they fall short, and what we need to improve.

You want to pay attention to the competitive landscape, but you can’t let it become your compass. The question is whether we’re making progress toward AI that people can trust and that broadly improves their lives.
